introduction_strategy.hook_hypothesis: Network physiology characterises how organ systems interact as a dynamic network, and Time Delay Stability (TDS) is its standard pairwise coupling measure, used to show that physiological networks reorganise across sleep stages and in disease.
introduction_strategy.problem_gap_hypothesis: TDS depends on three parameters counted in samples (window 60, lag ±30, tolerance ±1) chosen for 1-Hz sleep recordings; at other time scales or sampling rates they are a guess, fixed values can fail silently (high scores with wrong delays), and parameter differences hamper reproducibility. Scope: tested on synthetic signals with known coupling, a 35-subject sleep cohort and three records from other fields with known delays.
search_directions: Foundational papers introducing Time Delay Stability and network physiology during sleep (Bashan et al. 2012 Nature Communications; Bartsch et al. 2015 PLoS ONE)
Reviews or perspectives on the field of network physiology (Ivanov 2021 Frontiers in Network Physiology; Ivanov, Liu, Bartsch 2016 New Journal of Physics)
Applications of TDS to brain-muscle, brain-heart or cardio-respiratory coupling, including clinical populations
Open-source implementations of TDS and reproducibility of TDS results across implementations (TDSpy)

related_work_strategy.overview: Position aTDS against three bodies of work: how TDS and related delay-based coupling measures are parameterised; effective sample size of autocorrelated series as the basis for a window rule; and surrogate-data testing as the basis for calibrating the tolerance and testing links.

content_bullets: State that TDS depends on window, lag range and tolerance counted in samples, published values 60/±30/±1 for 1-Hz sleep data.

Introduce aTDS: window = 30 x max Bartlett factor, lag = half the window capped at half a rhythm period, tolerance = widest value with chance score + 2 SE <= 5 % on rotated copies; 4-of-5 rule unchanged; no labels used.

Key results from experimental_log.md: AUC 0.92 vs 0.59 at r = 4; equivalent/better than hand-rescaled where decidable; oracle better; ±30 gives wrong delays for all 50 pairs beyond 30 at scores 72-96 % while aTDS exact in 90/90; no false link in 20 uncoupled networks after FDR.
State scope: simulated signals with known answers plus real data (35-subject sleep cohort with mixed results; three records from other fields where aTDS recovers known delays).
Report the new evidence honestly: full-record estimators win on stationary data; aTDS wins for regime-limited and drifting coupling; no gain on 1-Hz sleep networks even stage-aware.

subsections.subsection_title: 2.2 Effective sample size of autocorrelated series
content_bullets: Bartlett variance inflation; effective number of independent observations.
Surrogate-data testing, cyclic-shift nulls, cross-subject nulls of Bashan et al.; Benjamini-Hochberg FDR.

Formalise windowed z-scored circular cross-correlation C_nu(tau) = (1/L) sum_i x((i+tau) mod L) y(i), tau0 = argmax |C|, 4-of-5 stability rule within ±tol, TDS score; aliasing limit tau_max <= (L-1)/2; sign convention (negative tau0: x leads).

Autocorrelation r_i(k) for k = 0..T/4; Bartlett factor B_i = 1 + 2 sum_{k<K_i} r_i(k)^2 to first zero crossing; L = clip(round(30 max_i B_i), L_min, 0.1T) with L_min = 61 or max(61, 2 d_max + 1), floor wins; step L/2.
Why 30: error 1/sqrt(n) = ±0.18 at n = 30, max of 30 noise lags ~0.47, 4-of-5 rule separates; convention not optimum. Why 61: lag never narrower than ±30.
tau_max = floor((L-1)/2), capped at max(1, min(P_i)/2) for rhythmic signals; rhythm test: highest autocorrelation peak after first zero crossing >= 0.3 and not at the edge.

Circular rotations (20 per pair, shift in [a, T-a), a = max(L, T/10), up to 50 pairs pooled over recordings); C(t) mean and SE; tol* = max t with C + 2 SE <= 5 %, scan t = 0..max(1, tau_max/4), stop at first failure; calibration_failed flag; 5 % is a budget, not a significance level; upper bound vs mean (6.7 % on new pairs with mean only).
